label: before
description: Two optimisations, both in `api/app/sweep.py` and `api/app/store_pg.py`, no behaviour change (`make test` and `make test-db` pass unchanged). (1) The events the scheduler plans for one case (a breach and its first escalation rung) are appended in one transaction, `PostgresEventStore.append_many`: one row lock, one log read and replay and one commit instead of one of each per event; if the batch is refused for any reason the sweep falls back to appending one by one. (2) `run_sweep_parallel` / `shard=(k, n)`: the open cases are split into disjoint slices by a stable hash of the case id and swept by separate processes, each with its own connection pool, because replaying every case is CPU-bound Python. Before is the single-process sweep at commit 960e628, the base of this branch; after is the same call on this branch. Same machine, seed and sweep time. Timings vary by about 10% from run to run on a shared laptop.
notes: A first run, on a busy machine and before the base had moved, measured 48 s for the 100,000-case single-process sweep. It did not reproduce on the quiet reruns (17 to 26 s) and is not used here.

A17 (this branch): `POST /scheduler/sweep` now runs `run_sweep_parallel` on a long-lived pool of worker processes (`SweepPool` in `api/app/sweep.py`, used by `api/app/routers/scheduler.py`). `SWEEP_WORKERS` sets the size, default min(4, cpus); `SWEEP_WORKERS=1`, or any store that is not Postgres, keeps the single-process `run_sweep`. The pool is created on the first sweep (about a second) and kept; the rows with Workers 4 and 10 in the first table are the route itself, called in process on a warm pool, so they include the service-token check and the JSON response. Idempotency and no duplicate events across shards are asserted on the route in `api/tests/test_sweep_parallel_pg.py`, and a sweep killed part-way is covered by `api/tests/test_chaos_kill_sweep.py`.

Is 100,000 under 5 s now met in the real route? Not reliably, and not at the default of 4 workers. Five runs on this shared 10-core laptop (other jobs running; Postgres in Docker on the same machine), full sweep with the day's 11,276 events, then the re-sweep that emits nothing and is what the 10-second loop mostly does: 4 workers 10.46 s / 5.58 s, 7.56 s / 3.59 s, 7.11 s / 3.92 s, 7.75 s / 4.63 s; 10 workers 8.51 s / 3.36 s, 5.34 s / 2.37 s, 4.99 s / 2.37 s (met once, by 0.01 s), 10.23 s / 4.34 s. Neither the single process (20 to 26 s) nor the default pool meets the target for a sweep that appends a day's events at once; 10 workers meets it only when the machine is otherwise quiet. A steady-state sweep (nothing to append) of 100,000 cases takes 2.4 to 3.4 s with 10 workers and 3.6 to 5.6 s with 4. The shortfall is CPU, not durability: setting `synchronous_commit=off` for the workers changed the 100,000-case figures by about 5% (inside the noise) and was not adopted.

Why more workers do not scale linearly: replaying every case and appending each event is Python CPU work plus one Postgres transaction per case, and with 10 workers the Python processes, the Postgres backends and the Docker VM share 10 cores. Ideal scaling from the single-process split (read and replay about 10 s, appends about 10.6 s) would give about 2.3 s at 10 workers; the measured best is 5.0 s. Lowering the figure further needs a cheaper append (the store re-reads and re-replays the log inside each append transaction) or skipping cases that cannot be due, both changes to `api/app/store_pg.py` outside this ticket.
